"executive_summary": "This study investigates the potential of crude leaf extracts from the plant Ajuga iva as a green control agent against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The researchers hypothesized that phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes present in the plant would disrupt insect development. Using castor bean leaves treated with aqueous solutions of the extract at concentrations of 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl, the team assessed mortality, growth rates, and gut morphology in first and third instar larvae. Results demonstrated a dose-dependent increase in larval mortality, reaching 85% at the highest concentration for first instars. Third instar larvae exhibited significantly reduced larval weight gain and relative growth rates, with none surviving beyond 8 days at the highest dose. Histological analysis revealed that the extract caused nuclear abnormalities and a reduction in actin filaments within the larval gut, suggesting direct toxicity to gut epithelial cells. Furthermore, larvae were unable to pupate, indicating a disruption of the molting cycle. The study concludes that A. iva extracts, particularly due to their phytoecdysteroid content, are promising candidates for integrated pest management programs, offering an environmentally safer alternative to synthetic insecticides.",

summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime; Galina Lebedev; Jackline Abo-Nassar; Sally Marzouk; Moshe Inbar; Murad Ghanim; Radi Aly
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the potential of crude leaf extracts from the plant Ajuga iva as a green control agent against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The researchers hypothesized that phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes present in the plant would disrupt insect development. Using castor bean leaves treated with aqueous solutions of the extract at concentrations of 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl, the team assessed mortality, growth rates, and gut morphology in first and third instar larvae. Results demonstrated a dose-dependent increase in larval mortality, reaching 85% at the highest concentration for first instars. Third instar larvae exhibited significantly reduced larval weight gain and relative growth rates, with none surviving beyond 8 days at the highest dose. Histological analysis revealed that the extract caused nuclear abnormalities and a reduction in actin filaments within the larval gut, suggesting direct toxicity to gut epithelial cells. Furthermore, larvae were unable to pupate, indicating a disruption of the molting cycle. The study concludes that A. iva extracts, particularly due to their phytoecdysteroid content, are promising candidates for integrated pest management programs, offering an environmentally safer alternative to synthetic insecticides.

claims.description: Crude extracts of Ajuga iva significantly reduce the survival and development of Spodoptera littoralis larvae.
Phytoecdysteroids in the extract cause direct damage to the larval gut morphology.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the potential of crude leaf extracts from the plant Ajuga iva as a green control agent against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The researchers hypothesized that phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes present in the plant would disrupt insect development. Using castor bean leaves treated with aqueous solutions of the extract at concentrations of 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl, the team assessed mortality, growth rates, and gut morphology in first and third instar larvae. Results demonstrated a dose-dependent increase in larval mortality, reaching 85% at the highest concentration for first instars. Third instar larvae exhibited significantly reduced larval weight gain and relative growth rates, with none surviving beyond 8 days at the highest dose. Histological analysis revealed that the extract caused nuclear abnormalities and a reduction in actin filaments within the larval gut, suggesting direct toxicity to gut epithelial cells. Furthermore, larvae were unable to pupate, indicating a disruption of the molting cycle. The study concludes that A. iva extracts, particularly due to their phytoecdysteroid content, are promising candidates for integrated pest management programs, offering an environmentally safer alternative to synthetic insecticides.

Research Context
Insect pests cause severe damage to numerous crops. Control relies heavily on synthetic pesticides. Pesticides pose risks to human health and the environment. Green control methods are becoming increasingly popular. Phytoecdysteroids affect a wide range of insects. These compounds mimic insect molting hormones. They can cause abnormal larval development and death.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study examined Ajuga extracts for pest control. We hypothesized the extract would interfere with molting. The first question asks if the extract affects larvae. The second question compares crude extract to standards. The third question investigates direct gut effects. The hypothesis predicts reduced development and survival.

Methodological Details
The study used the African cotton leafworm. Larvae were sourced from a specific laboratory colony. First and third instar larvae were used for bioassays. Plants were collected after blooming from July to November. Plant material was oven-dried at 55 degrees Celsius. Powder was soaked in methanol for extraction. Homogenization was performed at 2500 rpm for 1 hour. Extracts were centrifuged at 112 g for 10 minutes. Analysis used LC-TOF-MS and Thin-layer chromatography. Castor bean leaves served as the feeding substrate. Treatments included Tween 20 as a surfactant. Three concentrations were tested: 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl. First instar larvae were exposed for 3 days. Third instar larvae were exposed for 4 or 8 days. Experiments included 11 replicates for first instars. Experiments included 20 replicates for third instars. Statistical analysis used t-tests and ANOVA. Gut morphology was visualized via confocal microscopy.

Procedures And Architectures
Crude extracts were prepared using a published procedure. Purification involved vacuum concentration and aqueous treatment. Identification confirmed presence of three phytoecdysteroids. Compounds identified were ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone. Leaves were smeared with extract using a paint brush. Leaves were dried in a chemical hood for 2 hours. Controls were smeared with double-distilled water. Survival was compared to controls using t-tests. Relative growth rate was calculated using weight changes. Pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days. Guts were fixed in paraformaldehyde for histology. Staining used phalloidin for actin and DAPI for nuclei. Images were captured using Leica and Olympus microscopes.

Key Results
First instar mortality increased with extract concentration. Mortality was 25% at 50 µg/µl, 65% at 100 µg/µl. Control mortality was only 5%. Third instar larval weight gain was significantly reduced. Relative growth rate decreased significantly across all concentrations. RGR decreased by 0.05 and 0.20 g/g day at high dose. Survival was significantly reduced after 11 days. None of the highest dose larvae survived past 8 days. Survival was 10 days for lower concentrations. Purified phytoecdysteroid mixture also reduced growth. Few larvae survived on purified phytoecdysteroid fraction. Larvae lost weight and stopped growing at high doses. Gut nuclei became smaller and abnormal in shape. Actin filaments were smaller and reduced in amount. Larvae were unable to complete development and pupate. Incomplete pupae had short limbs and small heads.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Phytoecdysteroids negatively affect lepidopteran pests. Results agree with studies on herbivore survival. The extract showed a dose-dependent effect. Effects were observed regardless of larval age. Disruption of the molting cycle was observed. Suppressed pupation occurred due to reduced weight gain. Larvae did not reach the threshold weight for pupation. Gut histolysis showed clear signs of apoptosis. Microvilli destruction and vacuole formation were observed. Gut damage supports disruption of hormonal balance. Actin disruption may result from phytoecdysteroid titers. The compounds may be useful for pest management.

Contradictions And Limitations
Clerodanes were not fractionated due to difficulty. Fractionation was difficult and costly. Commercial standards were too expensive. Commercial standards could not match treatment concentrations. The mixture of standards had no significant effect. Standard concentrations were much lower than crude extract. Crude extract concentration was 250,000 ppm. High concentrations of pure standards are needed for effect. The study did not test clerodane activity directly.

Claims
Crude extracts of Ajuga iva significantly reduce the survival and development of Spodoptera littoralis larvae. Mortality reached 85% at the highest concentration. Larval weight gain was significantly reduced. Relative growth rate decreased significantly. None survived beyond 8 days at high dose. Purified phytoecdysteroid mixture at low ppm had no effect. Commercial standards were used at much lower concentrations. Extracts may be useful for pest management. They offer a green control alternative to pesticides.
Phytoecdysteroids in the extract cause direct damage to the larval gut morphology. Nuclei became smaller and abnormal in shape. Actin filaments were smaller and reduced in amount. Gut cells showed histolysis with signs of apoptosis. Control treatment showed normal actin-filament organization. Gut damage leads to reduced weight gain and mortality. This supports the disruption of hormonal balance.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation of clerodanes was performed by not fractionating them. Ablation of phytoecdysteroids was tested via purified mixture. The purified mixture showed similar effects to crude extract. However, the purified mixture was tested at lower concentrations.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows retention factor values of phytoecdysteroids. Figure 2a shows first instar larval survival rates. Figure 3a shows relative growth rate changes. Figure 3b shows third instar larval survival over time. Figure 4 shows RGR and survival with treatment order reversal. Figure 5 shows RGR and survival with purified phytoecdysteroids. Figure 6 shows gut morphology with phalloidin and DAPI staining. Figure 7 shows incomplete pupae obtained after treatment.

Three Takeaways
Crude A. iva extract causes high mortality and growth inhibition. Purified phytoecdysteroids replicate the effects of the crude extract. Gut histology reveals actin disruption as a mechanism of toxicity.
